transcript.reader:
Before we start, let me be sure I have the claim you're defending. You're saying: explain every function in the vicinity and the further question — why is any of it experienced? — is still open; nothing physical entails experience; so a theory of consciousness must add experience itself as fundamental, with new basic psychophysical laws. Is that a fair version?

Two questions, one part and one change each.

1. Take the central move: **experience is not entailed by any physical account, so it must be taken as fundamental.** Name one change to the world that would show that move is wrong — some result that could actually turn up, and where we would look for it. Then name one change that you say should make no difference to it at all. Both halves, please.

2. Your step from "it is conceptually coherent that any given process could exist without experience" to "therefore no physical account will tell us why experience arises" looks swappable. Hand me a near neighbour of that step that would work just as well — for instance, that it is conceptually coherent that a living thing could have all the machinery of life without a vital spirit, or that water could be H₂O without being wet — and tell me whether the same reasoning still reaches your conclusion. If it does, what does the step leave out that would have caught it?
transcript.author:
**1.** Fair version, yes.

**Where it could be shown wrong.** My claim is conceptual, so it is defeated by a derivation, not a datum: if a physical account of a system entailed facts about its experience — not merely its functions, but the presence and the intrinsic character of its experience — with no bridging premise smuggled in. Empirically, the place to look is the clinic: a validated, intersubjective marker of experience (a "qualia decoder") that read off the quality of a subject's experience from physical facts alone, and whose readings were independently confirmed rather than assumed, would remove the motivation for an extra ingredient. I would be extremely surprised; I know of nothing of the kind, and I cannot see what form such an entailment would take.

**Where it should make no difference.** Any physical detail of the mechanism — 40-Hz oscillations or Libet's extended activity, neurons or silicon chips with the same causal organization, chaos, or quantum processes. Swap the substrate, or discover new neurophysiology, and the further question — why is any of this experienced? — is exactly where it was. That is precisely the point of my critiques of Crick and Koch and of the quantum proposals.

**2.** The nearest neighbour is the vitalist one: "it is conceptually coherent that a system could reproduce, metabolise, and adapt with no vital spirit, so no physical account will explain life." That reasoning does not reach the analogous conclusion, and I say so in §5. It fails because "life" is functionally definable: all it means to be alive is to perform those functions, so explaining the functions explains life. The vital spirit was an explanatory posit, added to do functional work and discardable once physics did that work.

The water/H₂O neighbour cuts differently: if a posteriori necessity blocks the move from conceivability to possibility there, it might block it for experience too. I reject that (technical note), but I concede the explanatory gap survives either way.

What my step leaves out is the premise doing the real work: that experience, unlike life, is not functionally definable, and that "you've explained the functions but not the experience" is not a conceptual mistake. Whoever says "explain the report function and you've explained reportability" is confused; whoever says that about experience is not. That asymmetry is load-bearing, and my one-line inferential step conceals it.

transcript.reader:
Good — and thank you for naming the premise. Let me put the weight on that one.

1. On **"experience is not functionally definable"** — the premise you now say is load-bearing: what change to the world would show it false? Concretely, what would it look like to catch someone who *is* making a conceptual mistake when they say "you've explained the functions but not the experience" — same way we'd catch someone saying it about reportability? And which of your starting points could I believe *without* already believing that reductive explanation fails?

2. On the **double-aspect principle**: give me a near neighbour of "information" that would do the same work — "causal structure", "computational structure" — and tell me whether the principle survives with it. Then, for the two versions you say are still open (all information has a phenomenal aspect, versus only some), give me one measurement that would tell them apart, and one that both versions agree should leave the thermostat's experience exactly as it is.
transcript.author:
**1.** For reportability the mistake is catchable because "reportability" is exhausted by the capacity; someone demanding more has changed the subject. To catch the parallel mistake about experience, we would need to show that the residual question *cannot be posed* except by covertly changing the subject — e.g., a demonstration that our phenomenal concepts are implicitly functional through and through, so that a subject fully possessed of the functional theory finds the question "but why is it experienced?" simply unintelligible, not merely unanswered. Another candidate: a proof that "zombie" talk equivocates, in the way "reportable but never reportable" does. I have never seen such a demonstration, and I do not expect one; but that is the shape of what would defeat the premise.

On neutrality — honestly, very little. The functional analysis of the easy problems is neutral; the conceivability datum is neutral as a datum (one may conceive without conceding possibility); Nagel's "something it is like" is neutral. But nothing *entails* my conclusion without the contested premise that experience is not functionally definable. If you don't grant that, my argument gives you no reason. I would rather admit that than pretend to a neutral starting point.

**2.** "Causal structure" is the near neighbour that survives almost unchanged — indeed it is roughly what organizational invariance already invokes; it loses only the Wheeler "it from bit" hook and the Shannon notion of differences that make a difference. "Computational structure" fares worse: with it the principle slides toward functionalism, implying that implementing the right computation suffices — which I deny, since computation is defined by causal/functional role.

Distinguishing the two versions: no measurement does, in any direct sense, since experience is unobservable; we would need a validated marker. What would count: a principled organizational threshold below which every candidate marker of experience disappears while information processing continues — evidence for restriction — versus uniform correlation at all levels of complexity. Both versions agree that replacing the thermostat's bimetallic strip with a functionally isomorphic thermistor leaves its experience exactly as it was; only its existence is in dispute.

transcript.reader:
Two more, one part each.

1. On **organizational invariance**: your reductio says experience cannot change while causal organization and behavior stay fixed, because "there is no way for the system to notice." If the system cannot notice and nothing observable differs, what does this principle rule out that structural coherence alone does not? Name one change we could make — to the substrate, the organization, the report — that this principle says *must* alter the experience, and one it says *must not*, and tell me which of the two the switch-flipping experiment actually tests.

2. On the **limit you put on structural coherence** — that intrinsic character, the redness of red, is *not* recoverable from structure: suppose that limit were wrong and it turned out to be recoverable. What in your account breaks, and where would we look for the break? If nothing breaks, tell me which of the two it is: a claim about the world, or a decision about what you will let count as an explanation.
transcript.author:
**1.** Structural coherence only constrains which structures pair with which. It is compatible with two functional isomorphs having different intrinsic characters — it licenses the inverted-spectrum scenario. Organizational invariance forbids that: intrinsic character is pinned to fine-grained organization, so substrate is irrelevant.

What it says must *not* alter experience: replacing a neural circuit with a causally isomorphic silicon one. What it says must alter it: strictly, nothing — the principle is asymmetric. Same organization entails same experience; it does not entail that different organization yields different experience. The "must alter" half comes from a separate premise, that changes in experience correspond to changes in processing. Grant that, and rewiring the visual pathways so color information is routed differently must alter experience.

The switch-flipping experiment tests the "must not" case: organization is held fixed across a substrate swap, and the question is whether experience can differ. It never tests whether organizational change forces experiential change. That half is carried by the extra premise, not by the thought experiment.

**2.** If intrinsic character were recoverable from structure, the inverted spectrum would be impossible and the explanatory gap would collapse: explaining structure would be explaining experience. Then my §3 residual question dissolves, the nonreductive turn loses its motive, the double-aspect principle becomes unnecessary, and my "fourth strategy" — accounting for the structure of experience — would suffice. Nearly the whole architecture breaks.

Where to look: whether the recovery is a derivation or a correlation. The break would show up in an independently validated model that, given a system's processing, predicts its intrinsic characters — including which of two structurally identical subjects has inverted qualia, confirmed by a marker that is not itself behavioral. Without that, "recoverable" just means "correlated," which I already accept.

Which of the two? The limit — that there exist non-structural experiential properties — is a claim about the world, but thinly supported: chiefly by conceivability. The further claim that this blocks reductive explanation rests on a standard of explanation, which is partly a decision. If forced to choose: a claim about the world, held less firmly than the rest, with the decision downstream of it.

transcript.reader:
Two more.

1. **Add a job.** If simple information processing carries simple experience, what does the job of making *my* experience one unified thing rather than a crowd of small ones? Which part of your account does that work — structural coherence, invariance, or the double-aspect principle? And if none of them does it, could I run the same three principles on a case where the parts are unified and on a case where they are not, and get different answers?

2. **The best rival.** Take a rival that says experience just *is* the relevant functional/organizational state, with nothing added — the line you call "denying the phenomenon." Name one change to the world that would make your account and that rival predict differently. If no change on the list does, then tell me what separates you from them: a finding, or a decision about what counts as needing explanation?
transcript.author:
**1.** Nothing in my principles currently does that job. Structural coherence gives correspondence, not unification; invariance fixes what pins what; the double-aspect principle says information has a phenomenal aspect, but says nothing about why many aspects make one subject. This is the combination problem, and it is an unsolved open question in my own account, not something I can wave at. The most I can say is that global availability gives a functional analogue — jointly accessible information is integrated — and coherence links that to whatever unity experience has.

To your test: yes, I could run the three principles on both cases and get different answers at the structural level. A split-brain system has two streams of awareness, and coherence predicts two corresponding streams of experience. But that settles how unity is structured, not why there is a unified subject rather than a crowd. Those are different questions, and my account only addresses the first.

**2.** No change on any list cleanly separates us. Suppose a validated marker showed two functionally identical subjects with different phenomenal characters; I would call it inverted qualia, the rival would redescribe it as functional difference. Suppose no such marker ever appears; that is what the rival predicts, but it is also what invariance predicts, since I hold absent and inverted qualia nomologically impossible anyway.

So what separates us is not a finding but a decision about what stands in need of explanation. The rival holds that once reportability, access, and integration are explained, the residual question is confused; I hold it survives. I take the datum of experience at face value and pay for it with an expanded ontology; the rival buys simplicity by denying what seems most manifest. That is a genuine disagreement about methodology, and I cannot pretend an experiment decides it.

transcript.reader:
Two more.

1. **Where the parts came from.** For each of the three principles, tell me which of these it is: something you worked out with the target in view and would be caught out by a change you haven't tried (built); a pattern generalised from how the existing cognitive and neuroscience work already describes color, awareness and access (fitted); or something you simply laid down (asserted). Specifically, is structural coherence a *finding* you took from Hardin, Clark, Baars and the rest, or is it a requirement you brought to them — and was that settled before or after you looked at their results?

2. **The gauge.** Your account responds to every failure of reductive explanation by adding a fundamental property and a basic law — you say the explanatory burden is ultimately carried by those basic principles. What measurement would show that this move is swallowing a job rather than doing one — that is, what reading would worry you, and what would you have to see to conclude that "we posited a fundamental property" had become a name for our ignorance rather than an explanation?
transcript.author:
**1.** Honest scoreboard.

**Structural coherence: fitted.** The pattern — structure in experience corresponding to structure in awareness — is already there in Hardin and Clark on colour, in Baars on global availability, in any colour-space work. I formulated the principle *after* surveying that work; I did not have it beforehand, so I generalised rather than discovered or decreed. But I concede an asserted layer on top: that the correspondence is a *strong* constraint, that inverted spectra are intelligible, that it is nomological rather than conceptual. That layer is argued from conceivability, not read off the results. I have not tested it against much beyond colour, geometry, and intensity — unity and temporal structure are untried.

**Organizational invariance: built.** Worked out with the target in view; the dancing-qualia reductio is designed to generate it. It could be caught out — a principled biological chauvinism, or a demonstration that silicon isomorphs are impossible in a way that matters, would damage it. I flag that question as open.

**Double-aspect: asserted**, with fitted motivation. The isomorphism between embodied information spaces and phenomenal ones is a fitted pattern; that information therefore *has* two aspects is laid down, and I say so — speculative and underdetermined.

One built, one fitted, one asserted — and the fitted one carries the most constraining weight.

**2.** The gauge I would accept: whether the posits do work that is not already the datum. A fundamental property earns its keep by having independently checkable consequences — predicting structure, forbidding combinations, unifying with other domains.

So the worrying reading is *ad hoc proliferation*: each new fact about experience requiring its own free parameter, psychophysical laws written case-by-case, no economy, no restriction on which systems get experience, no independent consequence. If I kept adding posits — for unity, intrinsic character, causal relevance — and the list never tightened into one principle, then "we posited a fundamental property" would plainly be a name for ignorance, a promissory note on every unexplained datum.

Consilience would reassure me: if information is fundamental in physics, as Wheeler suggests, the same posit does double duty — evidence of a job, not a swallowing.

Concretely, I want psychophysical laws constraining neuroscience, invariance making checkable claims about silicon isomorphs, double-aspect linking to physics. If none were checkable, I should stop calling it an explanation. I cannot rule out that this is where it ends up.

transcript.reader:
Last two.

1. Given what you've conceded in this exchange — that the asymmetry premise ("experience is not functionally definable") is load-bearing rather than derived, that invariance's "must alter" half is carried by a separate premise and never tested by the switch experiment, that the limit on structural coherence is thin and partly a decision, that no change separates you from the functionalist rival, and that nothing in your principles does the unification job — is the claim you are defending now the *same* claim you set out to defend, or a narrower one? Which parts moved, and when?

2. What does your change list leave out — what kind of change are you making no claim about — and did you set that limit before or after you looked at what the methods of cognitive science could deliver?
transcript.author:
**1.** Same claim at the core, narrower in what it claims to support.

The content is unchanged: the hard problem is real, reductive explanation cannot touch it, and experience must be taken as fundamental with psychophysical bridging principles. I still hold that.

What moved was status, not content, and it moved during this exchange, forced by your questions rather than by any finding. I now say plainly: the asymmetry premise is asserted, not derived; §8's "planks in any satisfactory theory" overstates — one principle is built, one fitted, one asserted, and the fitted one carries most of the constraining weight; invariance's forward half rests on an untested premise; unity is unhandled; no experiment separates me from the functionalist. In 1995, "planets in any satisfactory theory" was too confident. The correct claim is that these are constraints any theory must accommodate, not that they are established.

What did not move is the argument that the methods of cognitive science are suited to functions and not to experience. That is the paper's core, and it survived the pressure.

So the negative claim survives; the positive theory was always flagged speculative, and you have shown me exactly how speculative.

**2.** What my change list leaves out: changes to us, not to the world. Every item — substrate, organization, report, 40-Hz, quantum, information — was a change in physical furniture or its organization. I made no claim about changes in our concepts, methods, or standards of knowing: whether a revised conceptual framework might deflate the problem, whether first-person reports could be systematically unreliable, or whether there is even a fact of the matter to report. I also left out unity and causal relevance.

On timing: the function/experience boundary follows from what the methods *are* — they explain functions by specifying mechanisms — and that analysis is logically prior to any results. But honestly, I drew that line knowing cognitive science had not delivered experience, and that absence is what made the line look like the hard problem. So it is not a pure a priori division. The structural point is prior; my confidence about where the boundary falls is responsive to what has and has not been explained. I am not neutral about that.

report:
# Report: "Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness" (Chalmers)

## 1. The question, frozen

The paper asks several things. I took the one its title and opening make central: **why does physical processing give rise to experience at all, and can any reductive (physical or functional) explanation ever answer that?** Range: any physical system, at every level — not narrowed. Kind of question: what produces it (forward), with a smaller backward part (what could we read experience off from?) and a scope part (what counts as an explanation). Frozen throughout; the owner did not move it.

## 2. The explanation in parts (owner's words)

- **P1** the function/experience boundary: explain all the functions and the further question, "why is it experienced?", is still open.
- **P2** the conceivability datum: it is conceptually coherent that any given physical process could exist without experience.
- **P3** the nonreductive turn: experience taken as fundamental, alongside basic psychophysical laws.
- **P4** the principle of structural coherence.
- **P5** the principle of organizational invariance and the dancing-qualia argument.
- **P6** the double-aspect theory of information.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Held by, or replaceable by |
|---|---|---|
| P1 function/experience boundary | **Held if** | Held only by the job "experience is not functionally definable" — a job the owner now says is *asserted*, not derived. What would settle it: a demonstration that the residual question cannot be posed without covertly changing the subject (phenomenal concepts turning out implicitly functional). |
| P2 conceivability datum | **Loose** | A near neighbour runs the same steps and lands somewhere the owner rejects: "it is conceptually coherent that a living thing could have all the machinery of life without a vital spirit, so physical accounts will not explain life." To stop it, he must add P1. So P2 adds no holding power; P1 is what is really held. |
| P3 experience as fundamental, plus basic laws | **Held if**, and the choice is **loose** | Held only through P1. The owner swaps "experience" for "some entirely new nonphysical feature from which experience can be derived" himself, and says only that the second is harder to picture — nothing stops it. Held if P1 holds. |
| P4 structural coherence | **Held**, and **loose** outside what it met | Held by the correspondence jobs it was fitted on: colour-space structure, visual geometry, intensity. Fitted, not built — it was formulated after surveying Hardin, Clark and Baars. Unmet changes: unity, temporal structure. There, loose. |
| P5 organizational invariance | **Held if**, one-sided | The "substrate swap must not matter" half rests on the reductio, which rests on "the system could not notice the change" — that is P4 again. The "organization change must alter experience" half is carried by a separate premise the owner names, and the switch experiment never tests it. |
| P6 double-aspect theory of information | **Loose** | The owner's own swap: "causal structure" does the job, losing only the Wheeler and Shannon hooks. So "information" is not held; something more general is. Its two open versions (all information has a phenomenal aspect / only some) can be told apart by no measurement — same explanation at this level. Settling test: a principled organizational threshold below which every marker of experience vanishes while processing continues, versus uniform correlation. |
| The unification job | **Unknown — no part does it** | Nothing in the three principles makes many micro-experiences one subject. Owner concedes this. Test: run the principles on a unified case and a split-brain case and see whether they differ *about a subject*, not only about structure. |
| Reductive rivals | **Loose** | No change on any list separates this account from "experience just is the functional state." The owner says the difference is a decision about what needs explaining, not a finding. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

**Flip.** Had a validated entailment arrived — a "qualia decoder" whose readings were independently confirmed — the owner says he would be wrong, in a stated way. Good answer; the claim sticks its neck out.

**Direction.** The negative claim runs forward. The positive work offered so far — neural correlates, global workspace, the decoder — is backward: identifying, not producing. The owner agrees, and says a full theory needs the bridge.

**Answer hidden in the starting points.** Partly. P1 is restated in three costumes: "not functionally definable", "an explanandum in its own right", "not an explanatory posit". The vitalism disanalogy does real work, but its force *is* P1. The owner now says so rather than citing neutral ground.

**Where the jobs came from.** Given: the experience question, the Nagel datum, the coherence data, substrate irrelevance, and (in this exchange) a validated marker. Added by me: unification, which he accepted.

**Pairs that pull.** (a) Economy against the posit: adding fundamental experience buys the hard problem and spends parsimony; the owner's own gauge is ad hoc proliferation. (b) P4's limit against P5: if intrinsic character escapes structure, and organization pins character, the line between them is where support is thinnest. (c) The two versions of P6: spread (elegant, counterintuitive) against restriction (needs a further free constraint).

**Catch-alls and gauge.** "Posit a fundamental property and a basic law" can absorb any failed reduction. Allowed only with a gauge; the owner supplies one — independence of consequences, restriction on which systems have experience, consilience with physics. The gauge has not yet been read.

**The change list.** Covered: substrate, new neurophysiology, chaos, quantum, 40 Hz, organization. Left out, on his own account: changes to our concepts, methods and standards of knowing; reliability of first-person report; whether there is a fact of the matter; unity; causal relevance. The function/experience line was drawn knowing cognitive science had not delivered experience — so the limit is not fully prior to looking. He says so.

**Rivals.** Vitalism: told apart by P1, so not independently. Functionalism/eliminativism: not told apart at all at this level.

**Where the parts came from.** One built (P5), one fitted (P4, carrying the most constraining weight), one asserted (P6); the load-bearing premise, P1, is asserted.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary

1. Give P1 a test: a case where "you've explained the functions but not the experience" is a mistake, and a case where it is not, with a rule for telling them apart. That single thing tightens more than the other three principles together.
2. Read the gauge: name one combination the double-aspect posit forbids, or one structure it predicts that coherence alone does not.

## 6. What this does not show

Hard to vary is not true. Loose parts may be true; the negative claim surviving the pressure says nothing about the positive theory. Also unresolved: which of the paper's weak points is the source's own (absences) rather than this report's.

## 7. One next step

Write the asymmetry premise into the paper as the claim's stated premise, and design one case that could either catch a subject making that mistake (which sinks it) or show the residual question surviving without assuming it.
